Data Acquisition and Preparation

Code related to Data Acquisition and Preparation goes here.

Code 
#' Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
#' 
#' This function will acquire and standardize all data for MP#01
#' from Netflix. Because Netflix hosts the data files behind a CDN, we
#' are accessing the release pages and automatically extracting links to the
#' relevant files (with CDN hash). 
#' 
#' After import, files are stacked vertically and some basic cleaning is
#' performed. 
load_netflix_data <- function(){
  # Note to students: Make sure you have installed the tidyverse and fs packages
  #                   before beginning this assignment. If you aren't sure,
  #                   simply run `library(tidyverse)` at your R Console and, if
  #                   you don't see an error message, `tidyverse` has been 
  #                   installed. (Same for `fs`) If you still need to install
  #                   either package, use the `install.packages` function as 
  #                   demonstrated in class.
  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)
  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
    
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
    
    return(local)
  }
    
  NETFLIX_URLS |> 
    map(read_html) |> 
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |> 
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |> 
    enframe("period", "url") |> 
   mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")), 
          path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed), 
          data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"), 
          data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |> 
    select(-url, -path) |> 
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4), 
           half=str_sub(period, start=6), 
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1), 
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 7, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |> 
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |> 
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"), 
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)), 
           .by=Title, 
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"), 
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"), 
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year, 
           period, 
           period_start, 
           period_end, 
           Title, 
           -half, 
           Runtime, 
           Views, 
           `Hours Viewed`, 
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`, 
           live_event)
}

NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()

# task 2, rename column names

NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data() |> 
  rename(hours_viewed = `Hours Viewed`,
         release_date = `Release Date`,
         available_globally = `Available Globally?`)


library(scales)

These column names had to be renamed with underscores, as using the original names with spaces would mean having to use the backticks when referencing these columns.

Code 
# task 3 - year into int, available_globally into boolean
NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |> 
  mutate(year = as.integer(year), available_globally =available_globally== "Yes") 
#glimpse(NETFLIX_DATA)

The data type of Year had to be converted to integer. Even though Year won’t have any math performed on it, it would still be useful to have Year as an int for filtering or comparison reasons. The data type of available_globally also had to be converted to a boolean for the same reasons.

Code 
data_start <- NETFLIX_DATA |> summarize(.by=period_start) |> slice_min(period_start)
data_end <- NETFLIX_DATA |> summarize(.by=period_end) |> slice_max(period_end)

The date range covered by this data set is 2023-01-01 to 2026-07-30.

Code 
non_distinct_shows <- NETFLIX_DATA |> tally() # 61892
distinct_shows <- NETFLIX_DATA |> distinct() |> tally()  #61852

min <- NETFLIX_DATA |> summarize(min(Views, na.rm = TRUE))
#min

There are 61852 different shows and movies in this data set. The full total of shows is 61892. There’s not much of a difference, but it’s important to distinguish because this dataset has repeat listing of the same season of the same show. Since this data set tracks content that has {r}min or more views, I find it hard to tell whether 61852 is a lot, given Netflix doesn’t publish all of their content in every country, and as mentioned, there are repeated seasons of the same shows, but in different periods.

Code 
bridgerton_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |> 
  filter(str_detect(Title, "Bridgerton")) |> 
  select(hours_viewed) |> 
  sum() |> comma()

bridgerton_hours

4,862,800,000 hours were spent watching content from the Bridgerton universe. This includes three seasons of the TV series, the Afterparty, and Queen Charlotte. There are repeats throughout the dataset and throughout the different periods represented in the dataset and I think it is due to the fact that Bridgerton remains popular well after a season is released. For example, season 1 might show up on the 2026H1 table even though season 1 was released several years ago due to high viewership. It wouldn’t hurt Netflix to keep producing Bridgerton material.

Code 
is_stranger_things <- NETFLIX_DATA |> filter(str_detect(Title, "Stranger Things"))
st_hours <- is_stranger_things |> filter_out(str_detect(Title, "Beyond")) |> 
  filter_out(str_detect(Title, "Tales")) |> 
  filter_out(str_detect(Title,"Fireplace")) |> select(hours_viewed) |> sum() |> comma()

5,548,500,000 hours were spent watching the five seasons Stranger Things. This number excludes spinoffs and Stranger Things: Fireplace. Just like Bridgerton above, the repeat listings by Netflix is included in this number. Stranger Things is still widely watched up to and including in 2026H1, similar to Bridgerton.

Code 
sum_top_ten <- top_ten |> select(hours_viewed) |> sum()
total_watch_time <- NETFLIX_DATA |> select(hours_viewed) |> sum()

watch_time_percent <- percent(sum_top_ten / total_watch_time, accuracy=.0001)
watch_time_percent
[1] "0.8089%"

0.8089% of total watch time was spent on the Top 10 titles of 2026H1. I interpreted Top 10 titles to mean the top ten most viewed, so for this, I created a filter for just 2026H1 content, then sorted the views. Then I had to find the TOTAL watch time of all content from 2023H1 to 2026H1.

Finally I used the total watch time of Top 10 title of 2026H1 and divided that by the total watch time of all of the content. With a fraction of 0.8089% for the total watch time of the Top 10 title of 2026H1, it doesn’t seem very high, however the titles that are on the list of top ten of 2026H1 are either Limited Series or a new season of an already well known and beloved show. I think that is reason for Netflix to continue investing in their more successful shows, but also branch out with some limited series, as they usually last for a few episodes so the cost to create would be lower.

Code 
# fraction of netflix catalog available globally, by hours viewed
global_by_hours_viewed <- 
  comma(sum(select(avail_globally,hours_viewed)) / sum(select(NETFLIX_DATA,hours_viewed)), accuracy=.0001)
global_by_hours_viewed
[1] "0.5192"

The fraction of Netflix’s catalog that is globally available is 0.3509177 by title, and 0.5192 by hours viewed.

Netflix’s globally available content by title is lower than by hours viewed, with half of Netflix’s content by hours viewed is available globally. Again, I’m more interested in hours viewed than the count of globally available content because the title count doesn’t assume anyone has watched the title or has even clicked on it.

I think Netflix can go either way on making region specific content. There may be some regions that have thriving local Netflix content that audiences would rather watch, than whatever other foreign Netflix content is available to them.

library(gt)


total_views <- NETFLIX_DATA |> summarize(sum(Views, na.rm = TRUE))

The first table is the top shows in each period by views and the fraction of total viewership it captured. The 2023H1 dataset didn’t have a Views column, so the tables I’ve generated will only reflect 2023H2 to 2026H1.

I also made another table using hours_viewed as the metric instead, to see if there was a significant difference and I thought it would be nice to include 2023H1 to analyze.

In my opinion, hours_viewed may be more informative than total views because Views seems to act more like a click counter, while hours_viewed takes into account content that are dropped as it shows how long people sit through the show/movie.

The first table is the Number of Title by period and the second is total content runtime by period. Content runtime is increasing while the number of titles by period is decreasing. There is a huge drop in number of titles from 2023H1 to 2023H2 so I’m guessing that Netflix either revamped their data reporting in between those two periods, dropped content, or lost streaming rights to licensed content. Since 2023H2, number of titles has been increasing by small amounts each period.

The increase in content runtime may be a result of the increase in number of content. 2023H1 is anomalous in that the number of titles is over twice as large as 2023H2, but content runtime is lower that 2023H2.

#3 Which shows have had the most consistently high viewership across all periods? 
#These shows are likely to be ‘staples’ that viewers fall back ... e.g., re-runs of Friends.

# compute the average viewership, the minimum viewership, 
#and the standard deviation of viewership across different periods 
#and develop a filter using some combination of these quantities.

# period_stats a table of the statistics (mean, standard deviation, and min views) of each period
period_stats <- NETFLIX_DATA |> group_by(period) |> 
  summarize(period_mean = mean(as.numeric(Views), na.rm=TRUE), 
            period_sd=sd(as.numeric(Views), na.rm=TRUE),
            period_min=min(as.numeric(Views), na.rm=TRUE))

Code 
# stdev_multiplier - adjust the number of standard deviations to move away from mean
stdev_multiplier <- 6
period_standard_devs <- period_stats |> select(period, period_mean, period_sd) |> 
  mutate(stdev_multiplied = period_mean + (stdev_multiplier * period_sd))
#period_standard_devs

# shows with viewership greather than the period's average + multiplier * the period's stdev
# default sorted by period.
inner_join(period_standard_devs, NETFLIX_DATA, join_by(period == period)) |> 
  filter_out(is.na(Views)) |> mutate(mean_plus_stdev_multiplied = period_mean+stdev_multiplied) |> 
  select(period, Title, Views, period_mean, stdev_multiplied, mean_plus_stdev_multiplied) |> 
  filter((Views > stdev_multiplied)) |>
  mutate(Views=comma(Views), 
         period_mean=comma(period_mean),
         stdev_multiplied=comma(stdev_multiplied), 
         mean_plus_stdev_multiplied=comma(mean_plus_stdev_multiplied)) |>
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(title="Views > Mean + (Multiplier * Standard Deviation)",
             subtitle="shows with viewership greater than the period's average + multiplier * the period's stdev") |>
  tab_footnote(footnote="This is the number that each title's View count is being compared to. 
               This number varies between periods. 
               It's the sum of the period's standard deviation times 6, and the period's mean.",
               locations = cells_column_labels(columns = mean_plus_stdev_multiplied)) |>
  tab_options(
    container.height = px(300), 
    container.overflow.y = TRUE  
  )
Views > Mean + (Multiplier * Standard Deviation)
shows with viewership greater than the period's average + multiplier * the period's stdev
period Title Views period_mean stdev_multiplied mean_plus_stdev_multiplied1

1 This is the number that each title's View count is being compared to. This number varies between periods. It's the sum of the period's standard deviation times 6, and the period's mean.

The 3rd and 4th tables are the list of shows with the most consistently high viewership across all periods.

The minimum View is the same across all of the periods, so I’m assuming that Netflix only tracks and records content that have at least that many views. And since the minimum is the same across all periods, I didn’t use minimum for this analysis. Instead, I focused on the mean and standard deviations.

In addition to using the standard deviation, I created a variable called stdev_multiplier, which is used to adjust the number of standard deviations to move away from mean. I wanted to capture the titles with the HIGHEST views, so I used the mean (of each period) and added the standard deviation (of the corresponding period) to try to capture the top percentiles https://lesn.appstate.edu/olson/normal_curve.htm

I continued increasing the percentiles to narrow the amount of titles further by using a constant (which I called multiplier): (mean + (multiplierstandard deviation)) I settled on a constant (or multiplier) of 6 –> ((6 x standard deviation of each period) + mean) I am comparing the views of each show to its period’s mean+(std_constantstd dev) to get the top top top tier content

The results are surprising because I expected to see Friends or Seinfeld, while there are other titles here that I was not expecting to see. It’s possible I did something wrong but the presence of Stranger Things, Squid Games, and Bridgerton slightly assuages my fears. In fact, some seasons of these shows appear on the list more than once, in a different period, so I don’t think the numbers I got were too far off.

library(gt)
#4 Within each period, what fraction of time was spent on ‘shows’ vs movies?
#hours viewed of shows / total hours viewed

#Length: anything over 4-ish hours is almost certainly a TV show, not a movie
#“Season”: if a title has “Season” in it, it is almost certainly a TV show

# total hours viewed of all content
total_hours_viewed <- NETFLIX_DATA |> summarize(sum(hours_viewed))
#total_hours_viewed

# 4 hours = 240 minutes
# filters:
# these filter out possible shows: content with < 240min runtime, or title contains "season"
shows <- NETFLIX_DATA |> 
  filter(Runtime >= 240 | str_detect(Title, "Season")) |> 
  group_by(period) |> 
  summarize(shows_hours_viewed=sum(hours_viewed)) |> mutate(total_hours_viewed)

Code 
#####

Tables 3 and 4 show the fraction of time spent on shows vs movies by period. There is a possibility that not all content were captured in the filter I had used to differentiate shows from movies: content with more than 240 minute runtime, or titles containing “season” are shows, content with runtime > 75 and < 240 are movies.

The total hours viewed of movies fluctuates while the total hours viewed of shows has been steadily increasing, with the exception of a small dip in 2023H2. The fraction of time spent on shows and fraction of time spent on movies show similar patterns. Overall, the fraction of time spent on shows is higher than on movies across all periods. The fraction of time spent on movies and the total hours viewed of movies don’t seem to follow any trends and look unpredictable.

It’s possible that the hours viewed of shows and fraction of time spent on shows are due to the fact that shows in general are longer and is thus able to hold onto an audience for longer. It may be worthwhile for Netflix to create more shows.

# 5 How does the performance of live events compare to pre-taped content? 

#Does the average live event draw more viewership than an average piece of pre-taped content? 
# Percent difference = (avg live − avg taped) ÷ avg taped × 100

# means of live content
live_ <- NETFLIX_DATA |> 
  filter(live_event == TRUE) |> 
  summarize(live_mean = mean(Views,na.rm=TRUE))

#mean of taped content
taped_ <- NETFLIX_DATA |> 
  filter(live_event == FALSE) |> 
  summarize(taped_mean = mean(Views,na.rm=TRUE))


# live average views, taped average views, percent diff
live_|> mutate(taped_) |>
  mutate(percent_diff = (live_mean - taped_) / taped_ ) |> 
  mutate(taped_mean = comma(taped_mean), 
         live_mean=comma(live_mean),
         live_percent_difference=percent(percent_diff$taped_mean,accuracy=.01)) |>
  select(-percent_diff)|>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title="Percent Difference of Live vs Taped Content, by Views") |>
  tab_footnote(footnote="")

#How about a ‘top tier’ live event vs ‘top tier’ pre-taped content?
#Does a ‘top tier’ live event draw more viewership than a ‘top tier’ pre-taped content?

# average viewership of live top tier content

#top tier mean of live content
live_top_tier <- NETFLIX_DATA |> filter(live_event == TRUE) |> drop_na() |>
  select(Title, Views) |> 
  mutate(live_) |>
  filter(Views > live_mean) |> #print(n=96) |>
  summarize(live_top_mean = mean(Views,na.rm=TRUE))
#live_top_tier 

# top tier mean of taped content
taped_top_tier <- NETFLIX_DATA |> filter(live_event == FALSE) |> drop_na() |>
  select(Title, Views) |>
  mutate(taped_) |> 
  filter(Views > taped_mean) |> 
  summarize(taped_top_mean = mean(Views,na.rm=TRUE))
#taped_top_tier

# percent difference of top tier content
live_top_tier|> mutate(taped_top_tier) |>
  mutate(top_tier_percent_diff = (live_top_mean - taped_top_tier) / taped_top_tier ) |>
  mutate(taped_top_mean = comma(taped_top_mean), 
         live_top_mean = comma(live_top_mean),
         top_tier_percent_difference = percent(top_tier_percent_diff$taped_top_mean,accuracy=.01))|>
  select(-top_tier_percent_diff)|>
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(title="Top Tier Live vs Pre-taped Content, by Views") |>
  tab_footnote(footnote="")

The average live event drew slightly more viewership than an average piece of pre-taped, if judging by percent difference of average live content vs average taped content. [Percent difference = (average live − average taped) ÷ average taped × 100]

Taking the mean of live content and comparing that to the mean of taped content, the percent difference is {r}live_percent_difference higher views for live content. I found this surprising because there was not much variety in live events (mostly just wrestling and baseball) compared to pre taped. The higher views for live content could be due to less live events but they have higher views, and the taped content could have outlier content that have really high views (or low views) that skewed the data.

When comparing the mean of top tier live content and mean of top tier taped content, the percent difference is {r}top_tier_percent_difference lower views for live content. I interpreted ‘top tier’ to mean titles that have viewerships higher than average, so I filtered by content that have higher views than the live/taped average (third table). Top tier live content has {r}top_tier_percent_difference less views than top tier taped content, which was what I had expected with the previous question, so it’s possible outliers skewed the data. A ‘top tier’ live event drew less views that ‘top tier’ pre-taped content.

I think the current mix of live vs taped content is a good mix. Even though live content doesn’t bring in as many views as taped content, live content probably requires less initial investment to make compared to taped content, so there’s probably a decent ROI.

Final Insights and Deliverable

For Netflix’s original content strategy for 2027 and beyond, I want to advise Netflix to invest more on TV shows. Going by the filters I had used above to differentiate between shows and movies (anything with season in the title is a show or anything over 4 hours is also a show, and anything between 75 to 240 minutes is a movie), I would say Netflix should invest more in shows, as the fraction of shows watched, compared to movies is about 10 times higher [part 6, question 4]. In fact, all of the top content by total hours viewed in each period [part 6, question 1] were shows, including limited series. The results of the top ten content of 2026H1 were also all shows and limited series.

I also want to mention that of the few repeated titles and seasons that appear in multiple periods, they were shows that are/were extremely popular, well known, and/or beloved enough to make appearances across the periods such as Squid Game and Bridgerton. To be more specific about my recommendation, I think Netflix should pay special attention to those shows as they are the ones viewers keep going back for to rewatch. My hypothesis is that content with longer runtime, such as shows and limited series, are able to hold onto viewers’ attention better and thus have higher hours viewed rate. Limited series would be nice to mix in, since a limited series doesn’t run for very long so there’s less cost in creating a limited series than a show, but still has a longer hold on viewers than a movie.

Looking at the trends over time, it doesn’t seem that Netflix content is losing any more or gaining any more viewership. While the viewership of movies fluctuates over time, it still remained somewhat consistent. As mentioned previously, movie viewership remains consistent over the periods of 2023H1 to 2026H1, at around 1-1.5% of total viewership. While shows have ten times as much viewership: ranging from 12-13.8%, and total viewership of shows has been increasing since 2023H2 by about 2 billion hours increased per period.

Another notable metric is that the total content runtime by period [part 6, question 2] and total hours viewed for shows [part 6, question 4] increased but the mean viewership by period [part 6, question 3] continues to decrease. Indeed, if the total hours viewed of shows and hours viewed of movies were added by period, the sum of these two do actually follow a similar pattern as the increase in shows by hours viewed, where it has been increasing every period, with the exception of a small dip in 2023H2 and another in 2025H2.

Increase of content runtime go hand in hand with increase of hours viewed, but decrease in mean views could mean that viewers view titles that have long runtimes. As mentioned previously, in this data set “Views” acts more like a click counter, so viewers are clicking on less content, but they stay watching that title longer. If the trends continue, I think Netflix should keep creating shows.

In general, Netflix’s shows beat out movies both in viewership and hours watched and it’s a constant trend throughout the periods in the datasets. The increases in runtime throughout the periods combined with the increases in hours viewed for shows mean that content shows have higher retention rates as viewers would have to stay with Netflix in order to wait for new seasons of their favorite shows to release. If working under this hypothesis, shows and limited series are worth investing more in, not just because of popularity but because with longer content runtime, there are more opportunities for Netflix to place ads throughout an episode, in addition to making more revenue off of subscription fees. Netflix movies just don’t draw as many viewers than shows, and that trend is reflected throughout the periods of the dataset.
